messages.subject: openCR question - how to estimate abundance for each group
messages.subject_clean: openCR question - how to estimate abundance for each group
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have run a model using "sex" as a factorial covariate and would like to estimate the abundance for each of the groups (females and males). However, it is unclear to us how we can do this.

(FYI: our question appears to be related to this (unanswered) question on phidot: http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=36&t=3949)

Underneath an example using the microtusFMCH and "sex" as a covariate to estimate phi. We used 'derived' to estimate N per session. The warning that is shown in the derived output lets us interpret the N estimates as calculated for all individuals, i.e., as if all individuals were females or males, depending in the factor level ("Warning: multi-group newdata; counts and abundance estimates refer to all animals"). However, how is it (is it?) possible to get the estimated proportion of females and males for the population at the level of a session (best would be with confidence intervals)?

#Example for a model with microtusFMCH data
#sex in phi
model_test_1 <- openCR.fit(microtusFMCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t+sex, b~t), type ="JSSAbCL")

#without sex
model_test_2 <- openCR.fit(microtusFMCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t, b~t), type ="JSSAbCL")

#get derived parameters
derived(model_test_1, all.levels = TRUE) #gives N estimate with included 'sex variable'
derived(model_test_2, all.levels = TRUE) #gives N estimate without included 'sex variable'

Thank you very much in advance!
Lukas

PS: I have run the same models using JSSAb instead of JSSAbCL and get the same results, which made me wonder. I thought only CL models work with grouping variables, or is this just true for spatial models?

messages.subject: Re: openCR question - how to estimate abundance for each group
messages.subject_clean: openCR question - how to estimate abundance for each group
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to expand my question a little bit as I have now played around with the models. My thought was that one should be able to use the estimates for the sex specific N  to calculate a proportion for each group and hence a “proportional N”. (Given that the assumption is correct that N is calculated as if all individuals were either F or M, see last email underneath).

In order to check if this works I also ran JSSAN models for each of the sexes separately. As you can see when you run the code underneath this strategy does not work. My estimated “proportional” N (from the original model) for females estimates higher numbers as for the separate model and for the males the numbers are lower, even outside the CI for one of the sessions. I didn’t expect a perfect overlap but somehow similar numbers.

Therefore, I tried another approach and used a JSSAb models separately for each sex (the same model as before) and derived() to estimate the N for each sex. However, this gives the same result as using the JSSAN model. Deriving the N is not the problem. The problem is that I don’t unterstand how to estimate N per group in a meaningful way using “sex” as a factorial covariate in the model (instead of running two separate models). Any help would be very appreciated!

Thanks in advance!
Lukas

Here is the code:

#libraries needed
library(openCR)

#Examples for a full model with microtusFMCH data
#sex-dependency in phi

model_test_1 <- openCR.fit(microtusFMCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t+sex, b~t), type ="JSSAbCL")

#get derived parameters
der_1<-derived(model_test_1, all.levels = TRUE)

#get females and males estimate
der_1_F<-der_1[[1]][["estimates"]][["N"]];der_1_M<-der_1[[2]][["estimates"]][["N"]]

#trying to estimate the real proportion of F and M in the data
N_prop_F<-(((der_1_F+der_1_M)/2)/2)*(der_1_F/der_1_M) #proportion females of averaged population size estimate
N_prop_M<-(((der_1_F+der_1_M)/2)/2)*(der_1_M/der_1_F) #proportion males of averaged population size estimate

#lets estimate F and M separately
model_test_FCH_1 <- openCR.fit(microtusFCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t, N~t), type ="JSSAN")

FCH_N_estimates<-summary(model_test_FCH_1)$predicted$N

model_test_MCH_1 <- openCR.fit(microtusMCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t, N~t), type ="JSSAN")

MCH_N_estimates<-summary(model_test_MCH_1)$predicted$N

#lets estimate F and M separately using the JSSAb model and derived
model_test_FCH_2 <- openCR.fit(microtusFCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t, b~t), type ="JSSAb")

FCH_der<-derived(model_test_FCH_2, all.levels = TRUE)

model_test_MCH_2 <- openCR.fit(microtusMCH, model = list(p~1, phi~t, b~t), type ="JSSAb")

MCH_der<-derived(model_test_MCH_2, all.levels = TRUE)

#get females and males estimate
FCH_der_2<-FCH_der[["estimates"]][["N"]];MCH_der_2<-MCH_der[["estimates"]][["N”]]

#plot the data
plot(1:6,N_prop_F, type = "l",ylim = c(40,100),col="red") #using the crude estimation for females from the model including both sexes

#underneath adding the lines for estimate and CI for the separate model for females (JSSAN)
lines(FCH_N_estimates$estimate,col="darkred")
lines(FCH_N_estimates$lcl,col="darkred",lty="dashed")
lines(FCH_N_estimates$ucl,col="darkred",lty="dashed")

plot(1:6,N_prop_M, col="blue",type = "l",ylim = c(45,110)) #using the crude estimation for each males from the model including both sexes

#underneath adding the lines for estimate and CI for the separate model for females (JSSAN)
lines(MCH_N_estimates$estimate,col="darkblue")
lines(MCH_N_estimates$lcl,col="darkblue",lty="dashed")
lines(MCH_N_estimates$ucl,col="darkblue",lty="dashed")

#plot the derived from both approaches - is basically the same as above without confidence intervals
#females
plot(1:6,N_prop_F, col="red",type = "l",ylim = c(45,110)) #using the crude estimation for each males from the model including both sexes
lines(FCH_der_2,col="darkred")

#males
plot(1:6,N_prop_M, col="blue",type = "l",ylim = c(45,110)) #using the crude estimation for each males from the model including both sexes
lines(MCH_der_2,col="darkblue")

messages.subject: Re: openCR question - how to estimate abundance for each group
messages.subject_clean: openCR question - how to estimate abundance for each group
messages.body_plain:
The derived estimates of N are Horvitz-Thompson-like (HT) estimates, using the observed number and their estimated detection probabilities. To derive separate male and female estimates from the joint model with sex-varying survival, use the observed numbers of males and females, and the session-specific detection probabilities (here not sex-dependent). Thus

Fn <- c(52, 53, 52, 45, 55, 72)
Mn <- c(56, 72, 49, 57, 46, 77)

FNhat <- Fn / openCR.pdot(model_test_1, bysession=T)[1]
MNhat <- Mn / openCR.pdot(model_test_1, bysession=T)[1]

#plot the derived from both approaches - is basically the same as above without confidence intervals
#females

#using the crude estimation for each males from the model including both sexes

plot(1:6,N_prop_F, col="red",type = "l",ylim = c(45,110))

lines(FCH_der_2,col="darkred", lwd=2)
lines(FNhat,col="orange", lwd=2, lty=2)

#males

#using the crude estimation for each males from the model including both sexes
plot(1:6,N_prop_M, col="blue",type = "l",ylim = c(45,110))

lines(MCH_der_2,col="darkblue", lwd=2)
lines(MNhat,col="lightblue", lwd=2, lty=2)

For a more complex model with variation in p you would need to tread carefully, using Nhat = sum of 1 / individual estimates. Perhaps there's a case for a new 'Nhat' function to do this. The ad hoc 'averaging' method doesn't work, as you found. Two other issues may mess up this analysis. By holding b constant across sexes you introduce a difference between the separate-sex model fits and the combined model. Also, the Microtus dataset has a lot of deaths on capture that openCR ignores.

I hope that covers it.
Murray

messages.subject: Buffer choice query
messages.body_plain:
Dear Murray et al.

I am trying to fit an secr model to my dataset on leopards in the Masai Mara using camera traps (see attached capt and trap files).

I have fitted sex as session and have some questions about that, but I will limit this post for simplicity to just buffer-related issues. The area over which I sampled is 510 square kilometres and the traps were placed between 3 and 5km apart. I understand that selecting the right buffer width is important for obtaining robust estimates. I would therefore be very grateful for your input regarding my buffer selection process as follows:

I have estimated buffer width as follows:
using suggest.buffer retrospectively (after running secr.fit using a buffer width of 3500m which is average trap spacing, itself based on half a minimum home range radius)
using esa plots
using the equation 4HNsigma again retrospectively
I don't have raster files to create a habitat mask but in any case the habitat in the sampled area is pretty homogenous ie savannah with occasional small patches of woodland
All this has produced a rather large buffer size of between 8000 and 9000m and therefore a lower estimate of leopard density than I had expected given the number of known individuals and the estimate previously obtained using MARK. This is assuming that in the real parameter estimates table, the numbers in row D are numbers of individuals per hectare as shown below

Fitted (real) parameters evaluated at base levels of covariates

       link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl

D       log 1.161568e-04 3.336264e-05 6.689452e-05 2.016967e-04 (= 0.0002 leops/ha)

g0    logit 5.643872e-02 1.337064e-02 3.527714e-02 8.912172e-02

sigma   log 2.735604e+03 2.697899e+02 2.255845e+03 3.317394e+03

2. When I reduce the buffer size to below 7800m, an RB >0.01 message appears which I believe means I have truncated the effective sampling area too much to have an unbiased estimate. However, the upper cls of the estimate using 7800 is lower than the number of individual leopards we actually detected! (i.e. n in Otis et al n, u, mt+1 categorisation)

3. I tried generating 6 different buffer widths and plotting these to see where the estimates of D stabilise (see Kalle et al 2011; Devens et al 2021) and this showed that for buffers of 6000m and above, the estimates are stable. This still gives a lower estimate than I think is the case but I am willing to go with it. I could either go with that (e.g. use 6000) or average the estimates from a range (4000-6000).

My questions is: does this process of buffer choice makes sense? Do you think I should ignore the RB > 0.01 messages?

Many thanks in advance

Bryony

messages.body_plain:
Dear Murray et al.

Me again, sorry.

As detailed in a previous post, I have leopard camera trap data (see attached files) over an area of 510 sq km. I have split male and females leopards (with a ratio of 6:7 [13 individuals overall]) by session, as you can see in the captfile.

I am assuming a half-normal detection function due to documentation suggesting this was the most reliable fit (and eg HR fits have long-tails and therefore are problematic). I am also assuming that I don't need to explicitly include b (g0~b) as traps were cameras and not likely to initiate a learned response.

I think in my dataset there may be heterogeneity in both the detection and state space parameters  according to #1 sex and #2 other differences between individuals, plus #3 I think there may be variation in detection over time (g0~t) due to changes in grass height over the 3 months sampled. I would therefore like to incorporate all these into the models.

However, the following is not possible (gives error messages):  fit<-secr.fit(capthist=leoCH, buffer=4000,model=g0~t+sigma~session+g0~session+g0~H2)

Additionally, the D estimates for males and females are identical (ie D~1) and I can't seem to prevent this. I tried using the predict.secr function to derive real parameters for each but it just gives the same ones as secr.fit.

Ideally I would like to test the impact of different parameters on model fits using AIC (e.g. testing my assumption about b, HN detectfn, sex variation and time variation). Presumably I could do this for simple non-nested models (e.g. g0~t versus sigma~session or g0~b with HN versus g0~b with HR) but I am not sure this would be valid? Also, presumably some of these effects may be synergistic as in general model selection and averaging in R and therefore comparison of either nested or complex models is appropriate?

Am I over-thinking this?!

Many thanks again
Bryony

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much, this helped a lot!

We tried to use the new insights we got from you (Murray Efford) to further work on our problem at hand. I am quite confident that we got it this time but, maybe it would be possible for you to have another look?

Below is the code using the FebpossumCH data and a model (“JSSAbCL") including time and sex dependency. The n_F and n_M (actual animals found) per session are used to derive the estimates and confidence interval. We had to slightly change the approach from yours as, we also wanted to calculate p-values (which we only have for the p on the occasion level - this is extracted using predict).

Thanks again!
Lukas

#libraries needed
library(openCR)

#Examples for a full model with FebpossumCH data
#sex- and time-dependency
model_test_1 <- openCR.fit(FebpossumCH, model = list(p~t+sex, phi~t+sex, b~t+sex), type ="JSSAbCL")

summary(FebpossumCH)

# hardcoded number of observed females & males
n_F <- c(64, 69, 61, 67, 66, 57, 60, 63, 52)
n_M <- c(78, 77, 86, 71, 63, 49, 73, 78, 62)

# hardcoded number of occasions
number_of_occasions <- c(10, 8, 6, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6)

# extract p values (for occasions) for both sexes
p_perOccasion_F <- predict(model_test_1, all.levels =TRUE)$p$estimate[1:9]
p_perOccasion_M <- predict(model_test_1, all.levels =TRUE)$p$estimate[10:18]

# calculate annual p values (numbers seem to match the expectation from former approach)
pa_F <- 1-(1- p_perOccasion_F)^number_of_occasions
pa_M <- 1-(1- p_perOccasion_M)^number_of_occasions

# calculating CI for annual p -> ??? is this correct ???
pa_F_lci <- 1-(1- predict(model_test_1, all.levels =TRUE)$p$lcl[1:9])^number_of_occasions
pa_F_uci <- 1-(1- predict(model_test_1, all.levels =TRUE)$p$ucl[1:9])^number_of_occasions
pa_M_lci <- 1-(1- predict(model_test_1, all.levels =TRUE)$p$lcl[10:18])^number_of_occasions
pa_M_uci <- 1-(1- predict(model_test_1, all.levels =TRUE)$p$ucl[10:18])^number_of_occasions

# Calculating Nhat using no. observed individuals and annual p -> Advice from Murray Efford
Nhat_F <- n_F / pa_F
Nhat_M <- n_M / pa_M

#calculating CI using the questionably calculated CIs for annual p
Nhat_F_lci <- n_F / pa_F_uci
Nhat_F_uci <- n_F / pa_F_lci
Nhat_M_lci <- n_M / pa_M_uci
Nhat_M_ucl <- n_M / pa_M_lci

Hi Murray,

Thanks for the reply!  Sorry for the delay in responding, was down with covid for a while.

I didn't realize I could so easily add an occasion-level time covariate to each session in the secr.fit call like that, so I just reconfigured my function to create simple T/F day/night occasion tables for each session rather than trap-specific day/night tables for each session.  Worked as expected!

Also, I'm sorry I didn't include my code; I thought it would end up being counterproductive since I have various functions that create the necessary secr inputs in the correct formats for each of the 168 sessions based on my capture/visit data tables, and my actual secr.fit runs are called by a group of other functions to enable everything to easily spread out and run across multiple nodes at the HPC here in Göttingen.  It's really been great to run my models that way... I could never have done it on my desktop but using thousands of cores at once really speeds things up and reduces the time-cost of trying out computationally intensive models.  :)

Thanks again!

Scott

> > So, a little bit of background first.  I’m working with small mammal mark-recapture data from 8 sites with 5 plots per site (40 plots total), that were surveyed at least once per year for three years, with some sites being surveyed twice per year.  The trapping periods consisted of 7 occasions generally, though some had as few as 4 and others as many as 10, due to extreme weather (either extra trap checks on very hot days, or closing traps during thunderstorms/etc).  The occasions correspond to trap checks either in the morning or late afternoon/evening, with mid-day checks added on hot days.  I’ve been using trap effort as a way to account for the day-time splits (i.e. 0.5 for morning and 0.5 for afternoon when there is an additional mid-day check) by specifying usage for each trap on each occasion (along with a reduction in effort for sprung/robbed traps, and sessions where number of traps used per grid was reduced due to lack of staff, etc).
> >
> >  I’ve been using multi-session runs of secr to estimate per-session density while including potentially important variables that impact the detection parameters, the idea being that as I’m running these per-species, I’d be getting detection parameters for each species and applying those across all sessions (site/plot/season).  This seems to work well, aside from requiring a rather long computation time (168 sessions in total when run together), but I’ve run into a snag trying to add day/night as a time varying covariate.  I’ve specified this as a factor for each occasion (essentially, were the traps mostly open overnight or during the day during that occasion).
> >
> > It seems as though there is a problem with having varying numbers of occasions between sessions, even though I have specified the covariates at the make.traps stage and everything runs and outputs ok if I do a single session (or multiple sessions that have the same number of occasions).
> >
> > Though it does run even with differing occasions, this warning comes up:

> > In `timevaryingcov<-`(`*tmp*`, value = timevaryingcov(allargs[[1]])) : mismatch between number of occasions in usage and timevaryingcov
> >
> >  And I haven’t figured out what to do with the error

> > Error in mat %*% beta[indx] : non-conformable arguments
> >
> > in terms of how to specify session in newdata to extract the predicted density in this case, assuming the warning doesn’t mean there’s a deeper problem.  It works with multiple sessions as long as the number of occasions is the same between them, but as soon as I introduce sessions with differing occasions I get this “non-conformable arguments” error (which is the same error as when I mis-specify the dataframe for newdata, so maybe there’s something in the data output that’s different that I’m missing, or it’s triggering the same error but in different ways?)
> >
> > In the end, I am interested in getting the best estimates of D possible for each session, and as activity for some species is almost strictly overnight, I think this day/night time covariate could be important.
> >
> > For the species I think would be most impacted, already the model including g0 ~ B is the “best” in terms of AIC, and g0 ~ t is even better (though I didn’t include it as I know this is technically incorrect to use, since the surveys were not all done concurrently, but it also could be a result of the general pattern of AM/PM/AM/PM/AM/PM/AM checks in each time series) which leads me to believe these are picking up on the fact that almost no individuals of this species are captured in the next occasion following a capture event (i.e. a transient response), but this is likely due to the alternating day/night periods and could lead to less accurate estimates when I have two daytime checks in a row rather than day following night.
> >
> > At any rate, I’ve looked through the google group and the phidot forums, and related answers helped get me to this point, but it sounds like there’s at least the possibility that there’s an underlying problem with how I’m interpreting the statistical methods, or a limitation in the secr package that I’m not understanding.
> >
> > I did see your potential solution for someone else with varying occasions in this case, where you suggested that they add “dummy” occasions to other sessions so all of them have the same number of occasions.  I’m a bit reticent to start down this path unless it’s really necessary… it seems like I could introduce other issues by filling this in across all my sessions.
> >
> > In any case, sorry for the long message but I wanted to include details so hopefully everything makes sense (or at least, makes sense enough to figure out what doesn’t make sense about what I did).  ;)
> >
> > Thanks in advance for any advice!
> >

messages.subject_clean: Adjusting for change in study area size necessary?
messages.body_plain:
I have a 14-year SCR data set on black bears based on DNA CMR in an area that was flooded during some years.  The flooding is reflected in the usage statistics for the traps for those years.  I am using openCR to estimate D and N, recruitment, phi etc. using a Pradel-model type.  My question is whether I should use the number of traps each year as a covariate on overall detection or will this be accounted for automatically by the usage data?  Previous analyses suggest that the majority of bears do not shift their home ranges because of flooding so I would not expect a big increase in density in the areas that were not flooded during flood years.  How should I estimate N from D for those years?
Thanks!
Joe

messages.subject_clean: Adjusting for change in study area size necessary?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe
Good to see you working on this dataset. When I looked at it a few years ago one of my hesitations was that I didn't have usage data for some spots that seemed not to have been sampled in some years (spillway 2007, 2011). Now you're onto it!

Usage data alone will take care of the differences in sampling - no need for a covariate. I'm not quite sure what you mean by a Pradel model type.

It's a puzzle how to estimate D (and N) when the extent of habitat changes between years because of flooding. My first reaction is that you could come really unstuck using an open model, because there are very specific unmodelled effects (limited temporary movement out of flooded areas, changing extent of habitat). If you are happy to argue/have good evidence that bears suirvive in situ then this is not an issue, and the open D-hat (N-hat) apply. I tend to place more trust in closed models for D (and N), anyway.
Cheers
Murray
